% Section: Constraint Composition (compressed, 787→~500 words)

At each decoding step $t$, let $G(t) \subseteq V$ and $S(t) \subseteq V$ denote the tokens permitted by the grammar and semantic layers, respectively.
The final mask is their conjunction:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:composition}
  M_{\text{final}}(t) = M_{\text{grammar}}(t) \;\wedge\; M_{\text{semantic}}(t),
\end{equation}
%
so a token is allowed only if it satisfies \emph{both} structural and type-level constraints.
The conjunction is asymmetric: $S(t)$ is defined only over $G(t)$. This reflects the enabling dependency (\S\ref{sec:method}): the semantic layer requires the relation type to belong to $\mathcal{R}$, a property guaranteed only by the grammar layer.

\paragraph{Grammar-First Fallback.}
When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$ (tight constraints leave no token that is both grammar-valid and semantically valid), na\"{\i}ve masking would force selection of a grammar-invalid token, breaking JSON structure.
We enforce a \emph{grammar-first fallback}: if no semantically valid token survives grammar filtering, semantic masking is skipped and the grammar layer alone controls selection.
Structural integrity is a hard constraint; a type violation is a soft error detectable by downstream validation.
Among type violations, DR and CF differ in severity: a DR violation renders the triple ontologically invalid (the entity type lies outside the relation's domain or range), whereas a CF violation means each triple is individually schema-valid but the same entity receives different type assignments across triples.

\paragraph{Constraint Tightness.}
Recall the tightness of relation $r$ (\S\ref{sec:bg:ontology}):\footnote{For symmetric relations, $|\sigma(r)|$ counts ordered pairs; the normalization $|\mathcal{E}|^2$ remains appropriate since we evaluate on directed triples.}
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tightness}
  \kappa(r) = 1 - \frac{|\sigma(r)|}{|\mathcal{E}|^2},
\end{equation}
%
The mean tightness $\bar{\kappa} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|}\sum_{r} \kappa(r)$ characterizes schema restrictiveness.
Tighter constraints eliminate more grammar-valid tokens at type-bearing positions; fallback frequency and residual DR increase accordingly.
This dual-factor pattern (tightness $\times$ baseline violation rate; $n{=}4$ model--dataset pairs, descriptive) aligns with the cross-dataset results: SciERC ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$) achieves 94--99\% DR reduction vs.\ DocRED ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$) at 45--90\%; the full range across three models is 42--99\% (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}; Appendix~\ref{app:dual-factor}).
The pattern extends to WikiEvents EE ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.82$; Appendix~\ref{app:wikievents-kappa}).
However, $\kappa$ is necessary but not sufficient for high violation rates: per-relation analysis shows that high-$\kappa$ relations with unambiguous entity types (\textsc{place\_of\_birth}, $\kappa{=}0.92$, DR${=}$0\%) have zero violations, while relations with comparable $\kappa$ but confusable types (\textsc{basin\_country}, $\kappa{=}0.97$, DR${=}$74.6\%) are highly vulnerable (Appendix~\ref{app:kappa-case-study}).
$\bar{\kappa}$ provides deployment guidance: schemas with $\bar{\kappa} < 0.5$ achieve near-complete DR elimination under zero-shot S1 (94--99\% reduction); schemas with $\bar{\kappa} > 0.8$ require fine-tuning to narrow the fallback regime (DR\,$\leq$\,0.09\%).
$\bar{\kappa}$ also determines post-hoc resolution feasibility: low-$\bar{\kappa}$ schemas ($<$0.5) benefit from TCR with negligible DR regression ($\leq$0.28\,pp), while high-$\bar{\kappa}$ schemas ($>$0.8) suffer harmful DR increases (up to $+$9.38\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).

\paragraph{Non-Rectangularity and Sequential Masking.}
\label{sec:rectangularity}
% Data source: artifacts/rebuttal/w2_rectangularity_report.md
Sequential masking is necessary because ontology type signatures are non-rectangular (0/7 SciERC, 23/96 DocRED relations satisfy $\sigma(r) = \operatorname{dom}(r) \times \operatorname{range}(r)$); independent enforcement would admit 33--37\% spurious pairs.

\paragraph{Zero-shot diagnostic.}
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: DR=0.1537; phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: R-F1=0.0823; phase2_scierc_full_s1: R-F1=0.0836
% bootstrap: delta=+0.13pp, CI=[-0.24,+0.58], p=0.5824
Full S1 reduces DR from 15.37\% to 0.93\% ($\downarrow$94\%) while R-F1 is unchanged (8.23\,$\to$\,8.36, $p{=}0.58$).
Per-relation DR drops to $\leq$2.82\%, reaching 0\% on 4/7 relations (Appendix~\ref{app:per-relation-landscape}).
Post-hoc filtering achieves slightly higher F1 via precision gains but discards up to 48\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:posthoc-extended}).
CF rises from 0.08\% to 9.90\% (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (b) Grammar layer
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Layer contributions.}
% phase2_scierc_grammar_only: RV=0, ET=0, DR=0.1484, R-F1=0.0823
Grammar-only eliminates RV and ET with no F1 impact while DR remains at 14.84\%, the ceiling of grammar-based decoding~\cite{geng2023gcd}; grammar-only CF is near-zero (0.08\%), so CF originates from the semantic layer.
Semantic-only reduces DR by only 24\% and cannot eliminate RV or ET; this is the \emph{enabling dependency}: adding the grammar layer yields a further 92\% reduction (11.65\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (d) S1 vs S2
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{S1 vs.\ S2.}
S2 achieves comparable DR (0.97\%) but lower R-F1 (8.03 vs.\ 8.36) with fewer triples (1{,}644 vs.\ 1{,}729) and does not resolve the CF trade-off (8.03\% vs.\ 9.90\%); we adopt S1 as the primary configuration.
% phase2_scierc_full_s2: DR=0.0097, R-F1=0.0803, CF=0.0803, triples=1644

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (e) Composability with Fine-Tuning
%  exp_ids: w5_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval,

%           w5_llama_docred_lora_unconstrained_eval, w5_llama_docred_lora_constrained_eval
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
\label{sec:composability}
Fine-tuning alone reduces DR to 1--2\% but leaves residual violations that vary by schema tightness (Table~\ref{tab:composability}).
On SciERC ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$), adding S1 eliminates or near-eliminates DR (DR\,$\leq$\,0.09\%): Qwen 1.95\%\,$\to$\,0\%, Llama 1.11\%\,$\to$\,0.09\%, with R-F1 within $\pm$0.1\,pp.
On DocRED ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$, 96 relations), S1 eliminates DR: Qwen 0.56\%\,$\to$\,0\% and Llama 0.49\%\,$\to$\,0\%; R-F1 changes are $-$0.10\,pp and $+$0.15\,pp.
Across all four model-dataset settings, DR\,$\leq$\,0.09\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp.
CF interference drops from $+$9.82\,pp (zero-shot SciERC) to $+$1.18\,pp (fine-tuned), tracing to \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X ambiguity (Appendix~\ref{app:cf-distribution}); the semantic layer alone accounts for 39--69\% of DR reduction under fine-tuning (\S\ref{sec:composition}).
LoRA + greedy S1 is the recommended fast deployment configuration: DR\,$\leq$\,0.09\%, CF\,$\leq$\,1.2\% at R-F1 40--46, with $+$10\% latency overhead (\S\ref{sec:runtime}).
Beam search ($k{=}4$) with LoRA eliminates all four violation types on SciERC for both Qwen and Llama (R-F1 43.60, 46.18; \S\ref{sec:beam-results}).

Usage:
    python plot_pareto_dual.py [--output beam_pareto.pdf]
"""
import argparse
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.ticker as ticker
import numpy as np

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Data: {beam_k: {"unc": {...}, "con": {...}}}
# dr/cf/rv in percent
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

scierc_data = {
    1: {"unc": {"rf1": 42.95, "dr": 2.11, "cf": 0,    "rv": 0},
        "con": {"rf1": 42.95, "dr": 0,    "cf": 0.50, "rv": 0}},

    8: {"unc": {"rf1": 43.17, "dr": 1.77, "cf": 0,    "rv": 0},

}

    1: {"unc": {"rf1": 47.28, "dr": 0.30, "cf": 0.19, "rv": 0.36},
        "con": {"rf1": 47.35, "dr": 0,    "cf": 0.19, "rv": 0}},
    2: {"unc": {"rf1": 51.31, "dr": 0.11, "cf": 0.05, "rv": 0.07},

        ("unc", UNC_COLOR, "Unconstrained", "o"),

    ax.legend(fontsize=9, loc="lower right", framealpha=0.9)
    ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3, linewidth=0.5)

    parser.add_argument("--output", default="beam_pareto.pdf")
